highlights.text: core meaning is an outcome and a place of return
Core verb: ṣāra / yaṣīru (verbal nouns ṣayr and ṣayrūra) — "to become, to come to be, to end up as."
Zuhayr's verse ("for eight years, over Salmā, upon the ṣīr of a matter neither bitter nor sweet")
core sense is entering into a house or the like
دَمَّرَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ ("God brought destruction down upon them"), and الدَّمَار (al-damār) means destruction or perdition
the مُدَمِّر (mudammir) is, per al-Shaybānī and al-Aṣmaʿī, one who enters the قُتْرَة (a hunter's hide)
Abū ʿUbayd, glossing the Prophetic report "Whoever peers into a people's house without permission has done dumūr," took dumūr to mean entering, but only when done without permission
highlights.note: a hadith, read legally by Abū ʿUbayd

highlights.text: a single root meaning one thing overtaking, catching up with, or reaching another
أَدْرَكْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I attained/overtook the thing")
their knowledge "overtook" them in the Hereafter, at the point when it no longer benefited them.
a single root meaning: something faint, low-lying, or worn away by use
the دَارِس retraces what he had already read, exactly as a traveller follows an existing road along its course
سَمْرَاءَ مِمَّا دَرَسَ ابْنُ مِخْرَاقْ — "dark wheat of the kind Ibn Mikhrāq threshed."
one coherent root meaning "to open" or "to split" something (fatḥ)
The base verb: fataqtu al-shayʾa fatqan, "I split/rent the thing" — a fatq.
attested in a line of al-Aʿshā's poetry: "At the door is a faytaq" (a carpenter)
soundness, setting-right, benefit
the difference/otherness of two things
هَذَا الشَّيْءُ غَيْرُ ذَاكَ = "this is other than / the opposite of that."
ghayr used for exception: عَشَرَةٌ غَيْرَ وَاحِدٍ = "ten less one."
Ibn Fāris cites a prophetic address to a man seeking retaliation, «أَلَا الْغِيَر» ("Will you not accept the blood-money?")
a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) indicating breaking, crushing and demolishing (kasr, haḍm, hadm)
hadadtuhu haddan means "I demolished it."
one root meaning greatness, loftiness, and setting-straight
الجَبَّار (al-jabbār) is what has grown tall and passed beyond the hand's grasp: a towering horse (فرس جبار), a date-palm too tall to reach (نخلة جبارة)
He cites a line of verse pairing this with "the loftily supreme one."
He quotes the Prophet's saying "the well is jubār and the mine is jubār"
He cites "and you eat up the inheritance with a gathering eating (aklan lammā)" (Q 89:19).
al-lamam is coming near to disobedience, and the word is used for a small offence
three unrelated base meanings: (1) crookedness, (2) the meeting of two things, and (3) casting something off
This is liqāʾ — meeting and the coming-together of two who face each other.
"It shelters a cast-off thing flung on a barren flat, scorched by the sun yet not melting."
to censure someone by attributing to him something blameworthy
لُمْتُهُ = "I blamed him"; the one blamed is مَلُوم (malūm)
to deserve or become liable to blame
(a) the soul that has gained some virtue and so reproaches its owner when he does wrong — ranking below the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinna)
a single root meaning: drawing something out in length, and joining one thing to another so that it extends
madadtu al-shayʾ, amudduhu, maddan: "I drew the thing out" (verbal noun madd).
amdadtu al-jaysh bi-madad: "I reinforced the army with a reinforcement (madad)."
a single sound root whose core idea is setting something up and making it stand out, prominent and upright
a stone that was set up and worshipped
al-naṣab: toil, weariness — because a person keeps standing upright (muntaṣib) until worn out
one's share or lot ("this is my naṣīb" = my share)
wealth "reaching the niṣāb at which zakāt is due," i.e. rising to that amount
Anything that has changed is called مُقْشَعِرّ (muqshaʿirr)
names the shivering/goosebumps that come over the skin from fright (fazaʿ) or similar
a verse describes a tent — "the tent of the family of Bayān" — as having become مُقْشَعِرّاً (muqshaʿirran, shriveled/desolate) one morning
one sound root pointing to a property of fire
a flame or firebrand of fire. Cited proof: the Qur'an, in the story of Moses — "Perhaps I will bring you from it a firebrand (qabas)" (Ṭāhā 20:10).
iqtabastu minhu ʿilman — "I acquired/borrowed knowledge from him"

one coherent core meaning: taking guidance or a "kindled light" from something (iqtibās/ihtidāʾ), combined with the idea of measuring or proportioning a thing so as to match it against another (muqādarah)
The same idea of matching underlies qudwah: an exemplar, someone who is followed or imitated
a single root meaning motion and agitation/trembling
Al-ra'd ("thunder") belongs to the same root
"Bluster beneath the thundering [cloud]" -- said of a man who talks a great deal but has no substance to him
"We had thunder and lightning" -- said when thunder was heard and lightning seen.
a root indicating agitation or unsteady motion (al-iḍṭirāb)
Al-rajj is setting a thing in motion: rajajtu al-ḥāʾiṭ, "I shook the wall".
two roots (aṣlān): a quality that is the contrary of coarseness (jafāʾ), and the quivering of something fluid
al-riqq, the well-known thing on which one writes
"she is cool with the coolness of a bride's mantle in summer, into which she has made the ʿabīr perfume run."
two distinct underlying senses: (1) elevation/height, and (2) return
a rise or elevated part of the land
a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rummah describing feathers rising above a *rīʿah* (a hillock)
commentators took *rīʿ* here either as "road" or as "elevated ground."
Two distinct roots: (1) a color, and (2) taking hold of something with the hand
"safaʿtu al-farasa" — to take hold of a horse's forelock
The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-ʿAlaq 96:15: "la-nasfaʿan bi-l-nāṣiyah" — "We will surely seize by the forelock,"
pressing straight forward, without turning aside or pausing
From the same root comes al-sumūd = lahw ("diversion, idle amusement"), and al-sāmid = al-lāhī, "one absorbed/heedless in amusement."
"It was said, 'Rise and look at them'... then leave aside your sumūd"
a single core idea: **intensity or severity in something, together with gathering/massing**
al-wabl and al-wābil = violent, pelting rain
Hence shayʾ wabīl — something grievous, heavy in its consequences
core meaning is aiming at something, intending it deliberately and making for it
Ibn Fāris cites Q 4:43, fa-tayammamū ṣaʿīdan ṭayyiban, "then make for clean ground/earth".
He cites the verse: "I aimed the spear at him sidelong, then said to him: this is valour, not the play of sliding games."
zalla ʿan makānihi: it slipped from its place (verbal nouns zalīl and zall).
zalla is an error, because the one who errs has slipped from the path of what is right
